From Middle English slicke, slike, slyke, from Old English slīc (“sleek, smooth; crafty, cunning, slick”), from Proto-Germanic *slīkaz (“sleek, smooth”), from Proto-Indo-European *sleyg-, *sleyǵ- (“to glide, smooth, spread”). Akin to Dutch sluik, dialectal Dutch sleek (“even, smooth”), Old Norse slíkr (“sleek, smooth”), Old English slician (“to make sleek, smooth, or glossy”).

senses.d: Slippery or smooth due to a covering of liquid; often used to describe appearances.
ex: This rain is making the roads slick.
The top coating of lacquer gives this finish a slick look.

senses.d: Sleek; smooth.
ex: Both slick and dainty.

senses.d: Appearing expensive or sophisticated.
ex: They read all kinds of slick magazines.

senses.d: Superficially convincing but actually untrustworthy.
ex: That new sales rep is slick. Be sure to read the fine print before you buy anything.

senses.d: Clever, making an apparently hard task look easy.
ex: Our new process for extracting needles from haystacks is extremely slick.
That was a slick move, locking your keys in the car.

senses.d: Extraordinarily great or special.
ex: That is one slick bicycle: it has all sorts of features!

senses.d: A covering of liquid, particularly oil.
ex: Careful in turn three — there's an oil slick on the road.
The oil slick has now spread to cover the entire bay, critically endangering the sea life.

senses.d: A rapidly-expanding ring of dark water, resembling an oil slick, around the site of a large underwater explosion at shallow depth, marking the progress through the water of the shock wave generated by the explosion.

senses.d: A glossy magazine.
